newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore paper report could revive Malaysia row.
newsitem.headline: Singapore paper report could revive Malaysia row.

text.p: A Singapore newspaper said on Tuesday that former prime minister Lee Kuan Yew was justified in his criticism of a Malaysian city for its crime rate, which sparked a fierce row between Singapore and Kuala Lumpur.

The Straits Times said it had analysed press reports of crime in the south Malaysian state of Johor, to which Singapore opposition politician Tang Liang Hong fled after January general elections saying he had received death threats at home.

Lee, one of a dozen members of the ruling People's Action Party suing Tang for libel, had said in an affidavit it was irrational to flee to Johor Baru, a city "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".
Johor Baru is the state capital.

Malaysia reacted to what it perceived as a major insult with fury. Lee, in a rare move, offered an unreserved apology. Kuala Lumpur still seethed, however, and Lee promised to have the remarks stricken from the record.
Kuala Lumpur accepted the promise, but stressed it would take time for the wound to heal. The Singapore High Court agreed on Monday to let him delete the remarks from the affidavit.

In his public statements, Lee never said he was wrong. In evidence to the court on Monday, Lee said he had based his remarks on newspaper reports that gave him the impression Johor was a dangerous place.
The Straits Times said it had examined those reports and concluded Lee was justified in his perception.
"An analysis of these reports shows that anyone reading them might well form a picture of Johor as being an unsafe place," it said.
It said in 1995 there were 46 muggings, shootings and car-jackings in the state. In 1996 there were 39 and there had been 12 so far this year, the newspaper said in a full-page report.

The newspaper said several victims of such serious crimes were among the tens of thousands of Singaporeans who regularly cross the causeway linking Singapore to the Malaysian peninsula to visit Johor.
It also noted that two policemen were shot and wounded on March 12, the day news broke of Lee's comments in what he had understood to be an affidavit not meant for public consumption.

The comments, released by Tang and Malaysian lawyer Abdul Razak Ahmad in Johor, enraged Malaysians. Many people took to the streets to demonstrate their anger, some carrying banners bearing insults directed at Lee.
